contexts.text: He said to him that did the wrong () = ... to him who is not in the truth of faith, and yet is within the Church. Explained.
Everyone wants to seem just and true... the wicked more than the upright, in order to captivate minds...
He supposes... that the upright would be more happy in the world than the wicked.
Jehovah is just, and I and my people are wicked () = that the Divine good could not endure the malice of the infesters... Their being wicked = malice.
Put not thine hand with the wicked () = no obedience to malignities... The wicked = one who is malignant; in the abstract sense, malignity.
For I will not justify the wicked () = that such malignity is contrary to the Divine justice. Explained.
The falsity of doctrine from the wickedness of the teachers.
For in proportion as anyone is in earthly and worldly things... he is in evils, and is wicked.

Not only does an upright man love what is good and just in another, but a wicked man also does so, because, with him, he is in no fear of losing his reputation, etc. But the love of good, with a wicked man, is not the love of the neighbour; for a wicked man does not love another interiorly, except in so far as he is of service to him.
For gifts from such an affection consociate both the upright and the wicked. Signified.

Nothing is more delightful to the wicked than to destroy the goods of love and the truths of doctrine, wherever they are; and to do evil to those with whom they are; for they burn with hatred against them...

The wicked form friendships, and consociate together, in order to inflict injury on the upright; it is the delight of hatred that consociates them: this makes them appear to be friends at heart, when yet they are enemies.
As infernal evil and falsity prevails with them, it is said, Set thou a wicked man over him, and let Satan stand at his right hand ().
